knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  message = FALSE,   # hide package start-up messages

# About this project

This notebook reproduces, one step at a time, the Visium HD analysis of *Arabidopsis thaliana*
seedlings published by Anita Shrestha in
[ashrest58-commits/arabidopsis-visium-hd-spatial-transcriptomics](https://github.com/ashrest58-commits/arabidopsis-visium-hd-spatial-transcriptomics)
(MIT licence). The data are the public 10x Genomics dataset *Visium HD 3′ Arabidopsis*
(Space Ranger 4.0.1 outputs).

I re-ran the whole analysis on a Mac in RStudio with Seurat 5.6. Along the way I fixed several bugs
in the original scripts and checked every number against the original. **This notebook reports the
numbers my run actually produced.** Where they differ from the original, the text says so and
explains why.

**The questions the analysis asks:**

1. Can we recover the tissues of a seedling (cotyledon, root, shoot meristem, ...) from gene
   expression alone, and do they fall in the right places on the tissue section?
2. Which genes have a spatial pattern?
3. Which genes and biological processes differ between tissues?
4. Does gene expression change gradually with distance from the shoot apical meristem (SAM)?

**Results at a glance (this run):**

- After quality control, 1,516 bins of 8 × 8 µm and 17,852 genes remain.
- Clustering gives 7 groups. Their marker genes and their positions on the slide match 7 seedling
  tissues: cotyledon, germinating seed, root elongation zone, root, meristematic tissue, hypocotyl
  and SAM.
- The most strongly patterned gene is **EXT3** (Moran's I = 0.79), an extensin expressed along the
  whole root.
- Cotyledon vs germinating seed: 331 genes tested, but only **50** pass both significance and a
  two-fold change. One gene (CAB1, photosynthesis) is up in cotyledon and 49 are up in germinating
  seed, many of them ribosome and chloroplast-building genes.
- GO enrichment recovers the expected biology: photosynthesis in cotyledon, ribosome biogenesis in
  meristematic tissue, cell wall in root, phyllome (leaf) development in the SAM.
- **AFO** and **ANT** are expressed only in a small area around the SAM, and both fall off
  significantly with distance from it (ANT p = 0.00026, the same as the original). **CAB1**, a
  photosynthesis gene, shows no significant trend (p = 0.14).

**How to run this notebook**

1. Open the project's `.Rproj` file in RStudio. This sets the working directory to the project
   folder, so the relative paths (`data/`, `results/`) work.
2. Run the chunks in **Step 1** and **Step 2** once, by clicking the green ▶ on each chunk.
   They are marked `eval = FALSE`, so pressing **Knit** does not reinstall the packages or download
   the 768 MB dataset again every time.
3. Press **Knit** (or *Run All*). The whole analysis takes about one minute on a laptop.

---

# Step 1: Install the packages (once)

| Package | What it is used for |
|---|---|
| **Seurat** | The main toolkit: stores the data, normalises, clusters, finds markers |
| **hdf5r** | Reads the 10x count matrix (`.h5` file) |
| **arrow** | Reads the bin positions (`tissue_positions.parquet`) |
| **Rfast2** | Fast Moran's I with permutation p-values (Step 8) |
| **ggplot2, dplyr, patchwork, ggrepel** | Plotting and data handling |
| **mgcv** | Smooth curves (GAMs) for the gradient analysis (Step 11) |
| **clusterProfiler, org.At.tair.db, enrichplot** | GO enrichment for Arabidopsis (Step 10). These come from Bioconductor, not CRAN, so they are installed with `BiocManager` |

```{r install, eval = FALSE}
options(timeout = 3600)   # R's default 60-second download limit is too short for big packages
install.packages(c("Seurat", "hdf5r", "arrow", "Rfast2", "ggplot2", "dplyr",
                   "patchwork", "ggrepel", "mgcv", "BiocManager"))
BiocManager::install(c("clusterProfiler", "org.At.tair.db", "enrichplot"),
                     update = FALSE, ask = FALSE)
```

> **Problem I hit:** the first installation stopped with a timeout. R gives each download 60
> seconds by default, and large packages such as `arrow` need longer, especially while the dataset
> is downloading at the same time. Setting `options(timeout = 3600)` and installing *before*
> starting the data download fixed it.

> **Why Rfast2 matters:** when Rfast2 is installed, Seurat computes Moran's I p-values by shuffling
> the data about 1,000 times. Without it, Seurat uses a formula from the `ape` package instead, and
> the p-values come out different (many become exactly 0). The Moran's I values themselves are the
> same.

# Step 2: Download the data (once, 768 MB)

**What Visium HD measures:** the slide is covered in a continuous grid of 2 × 2 µm squares. Each
square has its own DNA barcode, so every mRNA molecule captured on it can be traced back to its
position. Space Ranger (10x Genomics' processing software) then adds neighbouring squares together
into **bins** of 8 × 8 µm and 16 × 16 µm.

**Why 8 µm bins?** A single 2 µm square holds very few molecules, too few to work with. 16 µm bins
have more molecules but blur the borders between tissues. 8 µm is the usual compromise, and it is
what the original analysis used.

**A bin is not a cell.** Plant cells are large and irregular, and segmenting cells from the tissue
image did not work for this sample. So the whole analysis treats each bin as if it were a cell. A
bin on the border between two tissues can contain a mixture of both.

```{r download, eval = FALSE}
options(timeout = 3600)
dir.create("data", showWarnings = FALSE)
url <- paste0("https://cf.10xgenomics.com/samples/spatial-exp/4.0.1/Visium_HD_3prime_Arabidopsis/",
              "Visium_HD_3prime_Arabidopsis_binned_outputs.tar.gz")
download.file(url, "data/binned_outputs.tar.gz", mode = "wb")
untar("data/binned_outputs.tar.gz", exdir = "data")
file.exists("data/binned_outputs/square_008um/filtered_feature_bc_matrix.h5")   # should be TRUE
```

After extraction, the folder Seurat reads looks like this:

```
data/binned_outputs/
├── square_002um/   2 µm squares
├── square_008um/   8 µm bins   <- the ones used here
│   ├── filtered_feature_bc_matrix.h5   gene × bin count matrix (bins under tissue only)
│   └── spatial/                        tissue image, bin positions, scale factors
└── square_016um/   16 µm bins
```

# Step 3: Load the data into Seurat

`Load10X_Spatial()` reads the count matrix, the tissue image and the position of every bin into one
Seurat object. `bin.size = 8` tells it to take the 8 µm folder. The data end up in an *assay* called
`Spatial.008um`, which is why later column names end in `_Spatial.008um`.

```{r load}
library(Seurat); library(ggplot2); library(dplyr); library(patchwork)

obj <- Load10X_Spatial("data", bin.size = 8)
obj
n_genes_raw <- nrow(obj)
n_bins_raw  <- ncol(obj)
head(obj@meta.data)
```

Each row of `meta.data` is one bin:

- **nCount_Spatial.008um** is the number of mRNA molecules (UMIs) captured in the bin.
- **nFeature_Spatial.008um** is the number of different genes detected in it.

**Check:** `r format(n_genes_raw, big.mark = ",")` genes × `r format(n_bins_raw, big.mark = ",")`
bins. This is identical to the original (31,109 × 7,356).

> When you run this chunk, Seurat warns *"Feature names cannot have underscores, replacing with
> dashes"*. This is harmless: a few gene names contain `_`, which Seurat does not allow, so it renames them.

```{r load-plot, fig.height = 6}
SpatialDimPlot(obj) + NoLegend() + ggtitle("All 8 µm bins under tissue")
```

The capture area holds **several separate seedling pieces**. Keep this in mind for Step 11.

# Step 4: Quality control

**Why:** many bins sit at the edges of the tissue or on background and captured very little RNA.
Such bins are mostly noise and would form meaningless clusters, so they are removed before
anything else.

```{r qc-before, fig.width = 11, fig.height = 5}
summary(obj$nCount_Spatial.008um)   # UMIs per bin before filtering
median_umi_raw <- median(obj$nCount_Spatial.008um)

VlnPlot(obj, "nCount_Spatial.008um", pt.size = 0) + NoLegend() + ggtitle("UMIs per bin") |
  SpatialFeaturePlot(obj, "nCount_Spatial.008um", pt.size.factor = 6)
```

The filter keeps bins with **more than 100 UMIs and more than 50 detected genes**. Then it drops
genes that are not detected in any of the remaining bins, because they carry no information.

```{r qc-filter}
obj <- subset(obj, nCount_Spatial.008um > 100 & nFeature_Spatial.008um > 50)
obj <- obj[rowSums(LayerData(obj, layer = "counts")) > 0, ]
dim(obj)   # genes, bins
```

**Check:** `r format(nrow(obj), big.mark = ",")` genes × `r format(ncol(obj), big.mark = ",")` bins,
identical to the original (17,852 × 1,516). That means only
`r round(100 * ncol(obj) / n_bins_raw)`% of the bins are kept. This is a big cut, but the median
bin had only `r median_umi_raw` UMIs before filtering, so most bins really are nearly empty.

**Why no mitochondrial filter?** In single-cell studies, a high share of mitochondrial reads usually
marks dying cells. In plant tissue, metabolically active cells naturally have many mitochondrial and
chloroplast transcripts, so this filter could remove real biology. The original analysis skipped it,
and so do I.

```{r qc-after, fig.height = 5}
SpatialFeaturePlot(obj, "nCount_Spatial.008um", pt.size.factor = 6) +
  ggtitle("UMIs per bin after filtering")
```

> **Try it yourself:** change the cut-off from 100 to 50 UMIs and see how many more bins you keep.

# Step 5: Normalise, then check known marker genes

**Why normalise?** Some bins capture more RNA than others for purely technical reasons. To compare
bins fairly, `NormalizeData()` divides each gene's count by the bin's total, multiplies by 10,000
and takes the log (`log1p`). The log stops a few very highly expressed genes from dominating.

```{r normalise}
obj <- NormalizeData(obj, verbose = FALSE)
```

**Why check markers now?** Before trusting any clustering, it is worth confirming that known biology
shows up where it should. **PHB** (PHABULOSA) and **ERL2** (ERECTA-LIKE 2) are both expressed in and
around the shoot apical meristem. If the data are good, they should light up in small, specific
spots, not everywhere.

```{r known-markers, fig.width = 11, fig.height = 5}
SpatialFeaturePlot(obj, c("PHB", "ERL2"), pt.size.factor = 6)
```

# Step 6: Cluster the bins

Clustering groups together bins with similar expression. **It uses expression only, never
position.** So if the clusters later turn out to form coherent regions on the tissue, that is
independent evidence that they are real.

The steps, and why each one is needed:

| Step | What it does | Why |
|---|---|---|
| `FindVariableFeatures` | Picks the 3,000 genes that vary most between bins | Genes that are the same everywhere (housekeeping genes) add noise and no information |
| `ScaleData` | Centres each gene on 0 and scales it to the same spread | Otherwise highly expressed genes would dominate the next step |
| `RunPCA` | Summarises the 3,000 genes as 50 axes of co-varying genes | Removes noise and makes the next steps faster |
| `ElbowPlot` | Shows how much each axis explains | Helps choose how many axes to keep |
| `FindNeighbors` | Links each bin to the bins most similar to it (first 15 axes) | Builds the network the clustering works on |
| `FindClusters` | Finds tightly connected groups in that network (Louvain algorithm) | `resolution = 0.5` controls how many groups: higher gives more, smaller clusters |
| `RunUMAP` | Squashes the 15 axes into a 2D picture | For looking only: distances on a UMAP are not reliable |

```{r pca}
obj <- FindVariableFeatures(obj, nfeatures = 3000, verbose = FALSE)
obj <- ScaleData(obj, verbose = FALSE)
obj <- RunPCA(obj, npcs = 50, verbose = FALSE)
```

```{r elbow, fig.height = 4}
ElbowPlot(obj, ndims = 50)
```

The curve flattens at around 10 axes. The original used 15. Keeping a few more axes than the elbow
is safer than keeping too few, because a small tissue may only show up in a later axis.

```{r clustering}
obj <- FindNeighbors(obj, dims = 1:15, verbose = FALSE)
obj <- FindClusters(obj, resolution = 0.5, verbose = FALSE)
obj <- RunUMAP(obj, dims = 1:15, verbose = FALSE)

cluster_sizes <- table(cluster = Idents(obj))
knitr::kable(t(as.matrix(cluster_sizes)), caption = "Bins per cluster")
```

**Check:** `r length(cluster_sizes)` clusters, the same number as the original. `FindClusters` and
`RunUMAP` use fixed random seeds by default, so you get the same result every time you run this.

```{r clusters-plot, fig.width = 12, fig.height = 5.5}
DimPlot(obj, label = TRUE) + ggtitle("UMAP") |
  SpatialDimPlot(obj, pt.size.factor = 10) + ggtitle("Clusters on the tissue")
```

# Step 7: Find marker genes and name the clusters

## Marker genes

`FindAllMarkers()` compares each cluster with all the other bins using a Wilcoxon rank-sum test.
`only.pos = TRUE` keeps only genes that are *higher* in the cluster, because those are what define
it. For each cluster I list the top five markers that are at least two-fold higher
(`avg_log2FC > 1`).

```{r find-markers}
markers <- FindAllMarkers(obj, only.pos = TRUE, verbose = FALSE)

top5 <- markers %>% group_by(cluster) %>% filter(avg_log2FC > 1) %>% slice_head(n = 5)
top5 %>% summarise(top_markers = paste(gene, collapse = ", ")) %>% knitr::kable()
```

## Heat map: a bug fix that matters later

The heat map needs *scaled* values for every gene it shows, and some top markers are not among the
3,000 variable genes scaled in Step 6. So they must be scaled now.

**The original script scaled only the ~35 heat-map genes.** That replaces Seurat's whole table of
scaled values, so the 3,000 variable genes lose theirs. Moran's I (Step 8) runs on the scaled values,
so in the original it could only see those 35 genes. The fix is to scale the **union** of the
variable genes and the heat-map genes.

```{r heatmap, fig.height = 8}
obj <- ScaleData(obj, features = union(VariableFeatures(obj), top5$gene), verbose = FALSE)
DoHeatmap(obj, features = top5$gene, size = 4)
```

## Naming the clusters

Cluster numbers can change between Seurat versions, so **check the markers before naming**. The dot
plot below shows one key marker per tissue. The dot size is the share of bins in which the gene is
detected, and the colour is the average expression.

```{r dotplot, fig.height = 4.5}
DotPlot(obj, features = c("CAB1", "ICL", "EXPA9", "EXT3", "GRP4", "XYP2", "CYP78A5")) + RotatedAxis()
```

Each marker has its highest average expression in the cluster expected from the original mapping,
so I use the same names. Two markers are less clean than the others:

- **EXPA9** is highest on average in cluster 2, but it is *detected* in more bins of cluster 4
  (64% vs 51%).
- **XYP2** is highest on average in cluster 5, but it is detected in only 11% of that cluster's
  bins, and it is also expressed in root (cluster 3).

| Cluster | Name | Key evidence |
|---|---|---|
| 0 | Cotyledon | **CAB1**, RBCS1A, LHCB3: light harvesting and carbon fixation in photosynthesis |
| 1 | Germinating seed | **ICL**, MLS: the glyoxylate cycle, which turns stored seed oil into sugar in the first days after germination |
| 2 | Root elongation zone | **AGP31**, **EXPA9** (an expansin that loosens cell walls so cells can elongate) |
| 3 | Root | **EXT3**, XYP2, AGP4: root cell-wall and vascular proteins |
| 4 | Meristematic tissue | **GRP4**, NOP10, HDA3: RNA, ribosome and chromatin genes typical of dividing cells |
| 5 | hypocotyl | ACO2, AGP12 and **XYP2** (see above). This is the **weakest label** in the analysis |
| 6 | SAM | **CYP78A5** (KLUH), ERL2 and AFO, which mark the shoot apical meristem and young leaf primordia around it |

```{r rename}
ids <- c("0" = "Cotyledon", "1" = "Germinating seed", "2" = "Root elongation zone",
         "3" = "Root", "4" = "Meristematic tissue", "5" = "hypocotyl", "6" = "SAM")
obj <- RenameIdents(obj, ids)
obj$tissue <- Idents(obj)

# The marker table was made before renaming, so it still uses cluster numbers.
# Add the tissue names to it as well, because Step 10 selects genes by tissue name.
markers$tissue <- unname(ids[as.character(markers$cluster)])
table(markers$tissue)   # number of marker genes per tissue

saveRDS(obj, "results/annotated.rds")
```

> **Problems I hit at this step:**
>
> - `WhichCells(obj, idents = "Root")` failed with *"Cannot find the following identities in the
>   object: Root"*. `levels(Idents(obj))` showed `"0" ... "6"`: the renaming chunk had never been
>   run. Run `levels(Idents(obj))` whenever you are unsure which names an object is using.
> - Later, Step 10 failed with *"object 'tissue' not found"*. The `markers` table was created before
>   the renaming, so it had no `tissue` column. That is why `markers$tissue` is added right here.

**The real test is the tissue section:** do the named tissues sit where they should?

```{r tissues-spatial, fig.width = 12, fig.height = 7}
SpatialDimPlot(obj, cells.highlight = CellsByIdentities(obj), facet.highlight = TRUE,
               pt.size.factor = 4, ncol = 4)
```

# Step 8: Find spatially variable genes (Moran's I)

**What Moran's I measures:** for each gene, it asks whether neighbouring bins have similar
expression.

- **+1** means the gene forms patches (neighbours are alike).
- **0** means random scatter.
- **−1** means a checkerboard (neighbours are opposite).

It uses **only positions and expression, never the cluster labels**, so it is an independent way of
finding spatial structure.

```{r moran}
obj <- FindSpatiallyVariableFeatures(obj, features = VariableFeatures(obj),
                                     selection.method = "moransi", verbose = FALSE)
svg <- SVFInfo(obj, method = "moransi")
svg <- svg[!is.na(svg$MoransI_p.value), ]                  # genes that could not be tested
svg$p.adj <- p.adjust(svg$MoransI_p.value, method = "BH")  # correct for testing 3,000 genes
svg <- svg[order(svg$p.adj, -svg$MoransI_observed), ]
n_svg <- sum(svg$p.adj < 0.05)

knitr::kable(signif(head(svg, 10), 3), caption = "Top 10 spatially variable genes")
```

**Why sort by p-value and then by Moran's I?** With about 1,000 shuffles, the smallest p-value the
test can return is about 0.001, and many genes hit that floor. So the p-value alone cannot rank the
top genes; Moran's I breaks the ties. In total, `r format(n_svg, big.mark = ",")` of `r format(nrow(svg), big.mark = ",")` tested genes are
significant (adjusted p < 0.05).

**Check:** EXT3 is on top with Moran's I = `r round(svg["EXT3", "MoransI_observed"], 4)`, and AGP31
has `r round(svg["AGP31", "MoransI_observed"], 4)`. Both are identical to the original.

> **Honest correction:** in the original top-20 list, AGP31 is second. That list was drawn from only
> the ~35 heat-map genes, because of the scaling bug explained in Step 7. Ranked over all 3,000
> variable genes, AGP31 is in **5th** place. AT1G26380, AT4G18205 and IGMT2 come before it. RGF2 and
> RGF3, two root-meristem growth factors, also appear in the top 10, which is a good biological sign.

```{r moran-plot, fig.width = 12, fig.height = 8}
SpatialFeaturePlot(obj, rownames(svg)[1:6], pt.size.factor = 6, ncol = 3)
```

## Spatially patterned does not mean specific to one cluster

The table below shows where the bins expressing each gene fall: for each gene, the percentage of
its expressing bins that lie in each tissue.

```{r moran-overlap}
overlap <- sapply(c("EXT3", "XYP2", "AGP31"), function(g) {
  expressing <- FetchData(obj, vars = g)[, 1] > 0
  round(100 * prop.table(table(Idents(obj)[expressing])), 1)
})
knitr::kable(overlap, caption = "% of each gene's expressing bins found in each tissue")
```

EXT3 has the strongest spatial pattern of all genes, yet only `r overlap["Root", "EXT3"]`% of its
bins are in the Root cluster. Most of the rest are in the root elongation zone: EXT3 marks the
**whole root**, which spans two clusters. XYP2 is more cluster-specific
(`r overlap["Root", "XYP2"]`% in Root). A high Moran's I means "spatially clumped", not "specific to
one cluster".

# Step 9: Differential expression between two tissues

`FindMarkers()` compares two groups of bins directly, here **Cotyledon vs Germinating seed**, using
a Wilcoxon rank-sum test.

- `min.pct = 0.1` only tests genes detected in at least 10% of the bins of one of the two groups.
- `logfc.threshold = 0.25` only tests genes with at least a small difference between the groups.

Both settings are pre-filters that save time. They do **not** decide significance.

```{r de}
de <- FindMarkers(obj, ident.1 = "Cotyledon", ident.2 = "Germinating seed",
                  min.pct = 0.1, logfc.threshold = 0.25, verbose = FALSE)
de$gene <- rownames(de)
de$sig <- ifelse(de$p_val_adj < 0.05 & de$avg_log2FC >  1, "Up in Cotyledon",
          ifelse(de$p_val_adj < 0.05 & de$avg_log2FC < -1, "Up in Germinating seed",
                 "Not significant"))
write.csv(de, "results/DE_cot_vs_germ.csv", row.names = FALSE)

c(genes_tested = nrow(de), adjusted_p_below_0.05 = sum(de$p_val_adj < 0.05))
table(de$sig)
```

> **Honest correction:** the original reports this comparison as "330 DEGs". That is the number of
> genes **tested** (rows returned by `FindMarkers`), not the number of differentially expressed
> genes. In this run, `r nrow(de)` genes were tested and `r sum(de$p_val_adj < 0.05)` have an
> adjusted p < 0.05. Only `r sum(de$sig != "Not significant")` also differ at least two-fold
> (|log2FC| > 1). The difference between 330 and 331 tested genes comes from the newer Seurat
> version.

**The largest fold changes are not the most reliable.** The genes with the biggest fold changes are
detected in only a few bins, so they are not significant:

```{r de-top-fc}
de %>% arrange(-avg_log2FC) %>% head(5) %>%
  dplyr::select(gene, avg_log2FC, pct.1, pct.2, p_val_adj) %>%
  mutate(across(where(is.numeric), ~ signif(.x, 3)),
         p_val_adj = formatC(p_val_adj, format = "g", digits = 2)) %>% knitr::kable(row.names = FALSE)
```

For example, CA1 is 5.7 times higher in cotyledon, but it is detected in only 11% of cotyledon bins
against 4% of germinating-seed bins, and its adjusted p is 0.5. The genes that pass both cut-offs:

```{r de-significant}
de %>% filter(sig != "Not significant") %>% arrange(p_val_adj) %>% head(15) %>%
  dplyr::select(gene, sig, avg_log2FC, pct.1, pct.2, p_val_adj) %>%
  mutate(across(where(is.numeric), ~ signif(.x, 3)),
         p_val_adj = formatC(p_val_adj, format = "g", digits = 2)) %>% knitr::kable(row.names = FALSE)
```

```{r volcano, fig.height = 6}
to_label <- de %>% filter(sig != "Not significant") %>% arrange(p_val_adj) %>% head(12)
ggplot(de, aes(avg_log2FC, -log10(p_val_adj + 1e-300), colour = sig)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.6) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = c(-1, 1), linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey60") +
  geom_hline(yintercept = -log10(0.05), linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey60") +
  ggrepel::geom_text_repel(data = to_label, aes(label = gene), size = 3, show.legend = FALSE) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("Not significant" = "grey70", "Up in Cotyledon" = "#1b9e77",
                                 "Up in Germinating seed" = "#d95f02")) +
  labs(x = "log2 fold change (positive = higher in Cotyledon)", y = "-log10 adjusted p",
       colour = NULL, title = "Cotyledon vs Germinating seed") +
  theme_classic()
```

`+ 1e-300` avoids `log10(0)`. Some p-values are so small that R stores them as exactly 0, and
without this those points would disappear from the plot.

**What the result means:** only **CAB1** (light harvesting) is significantly higher in cotyledon,
and it is detected at a similar rate in both tissues (62% vs 63%). The cotyledon differs mainly in
*how much* photosynthesis mRNA it has. The 49 genes higher in the germinating seed include many
ribosomal proteins (RPL12-C, RPL16B, RPS11-BETA), nucleolar genes (NUC-L1) and chloroplast-building
genes (PORA, ALB3, CHL-CPN10, CLPP3). This fits young tissue that is still building its
protein-synthesis and chloroplast machinery. The glyoxylate-cycle genes ICL and MLS are also
strongly significant (adjusted p below 1e-11), but just under the two-fold cut-off.

```{r de-spatial, fig.width = 12, fig.height = 8}
top_germ <- de %>% filter(sig == "Up in Germinating seed") %>% arrange(p_val_adj) %>% head(4)
SpatialFeaturePlot(obj, c("CAB1", "ICL", top_germ$gene), pt.size.factor = 6, ncol = 3)
```

> **Caveat:** bins are not independent biological replicates. They all come from one section of
> one sample, so these p-values describe *this slide*, not Arabidopsis seedlings in general. The
> p-values are also over-confident, because neighbouring bins are not independent.

# Step 10: Pathway analysis (GO enrichment)

There are two flavours of GO (Gene Ontology) enrichment, and they answer different questions.

- **ORA (over-representation analysis)** takes a *list* of genes, for example the strong markers of
  one tissue. It asks which GO terms appear in that list more often than expected by chance.
- **GSEA (gene set enrichment analysis)** takes *all* genes of a comparison, *ranked* by fold change.
  It asks whether the genes of a GO term pile up at the top or the bottom of the ranking.

## ORA: which processes characterise each tissue?

**Choosing each tissue's gene list:** markers with adjusted p < 0.05, at least two-fold higher
(`avg_log2FC > 1`) and detected in more than 25% of the tissue's bins. Two tissues get special
cut-offs:

- **Meristematic tissue** has hundreds of markers, so it gets a stricter cut-off (log2FC > 1.5,
  detected in more than 40%) to keep only the strongest ones.
- **Hypocotyl** has very few strong markers, so it gets a looser one (log2FC > 0.5, detected in
  more than 10%).

**The background (`universe`)** is every gene detected on this slide. Only those genes could ever
have become markers, so using the whole genome as background would exaggerate enrichment.

```{r ora}
library(clusterProfiler); library(org.At.tair.db); library(enrichplot)

sel <- markers %>% filter(p_val_adj < 0.05) %>%
  filter(case_when(tissue == "Meristematic tissue" ~ avg_log2FC > 1.5 & pct.1 > 0.40,
                   tissue == "hypocotyl"           ~ avg_log2FC > 0.5 & pct.1 > 0.10,
                   TRUE                            ~ avg_log2FC > 1.0 & pct.1 > 0.25))
table(sel$tissue)   # genes per tissue going into ORA

ora <- compareCluster(split(sel$gene, sel$tissue), fun = "enrichGO",
                      OrgDb = org.At.tair.db, keyType = "SYMBOL", ont = "BP",
                      universe = rownames(obj), pvalueCutoff = 0.05, qvalueCutoff = 0.05)
ora <- simplify(ora, cutoff = 0.7)   # drop near-duplicate GO terms (similarity > 0.7)
```

**Why `simplify()`?** GO terms are nested and overlap heavily. For example, "rRNA processing" sits
inside "ribosome biogenesis". `simplify()` keeps the most significant term from each group of very
similar terms.

```{r ora-plot, fig.width = 10, fig.height = 8}
dotplot(ora, showCategory = 5) +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1)) +
  ggtitle("GO biological processes enriched in each tissue's markers")
```

The numbers under each tissue are the genes that could be matched to GO annotations.

```{r ora-table}
as.data.frame(ora) %>% group_by(Cluster) %>% slice_min(p.adjust, n = 3, with_ties = FALSE) %>%
  dplyr::select(Cluster, Description, GeneRatio, p.adjust) %>%
  mutate(p.adjust = formatC(p.adjust, format = "g", digits = 2)) %>% knitr::kable()
```

> **Why `dplyr::select` and not just `select`?** Loading clusterProfiler also loads AnnotationDbi
> and IRanges. These packages have their own `select()`, `slice()` and `rename()` functions, which
> *mask* dplyr's versions. Writing `dplyr::select()` makes R use the dplyr one.

**Interpretation:** each tissue gets the processes you would expect.

- Cotyledon: photosynthesis.
- Meristematic tissue: translation, ribosome biogenesis and rRNA processing, the protein-making
  machinery of dividing cells.
- Root: cell wall organisation and cellulose.
- SAM: phyllome development (*phyllome* means leaves and leaf-like organs).

> **Honest correction: hypocotyl has no enriched terms here, but 5 in the original.** In the
> original script, the special hypocotyl and meristematic cut-offs never took effect. The markers
> file stored cluster *numbers* (0–6), while the filter looked for tissue *names*. So every tissue
> got the default cut-off, which left hypocotyl with only 2 annotated genes. With so few genes, one
> or two hits can make a term look significant. Here the looser cut-off does apply: hypocotyl gets
> 15 genes, and none of its GO terms reaches adjusted p < 0.05 (the best is 0.15). Its top terms,
> such as "response to starvation", are the same as in the original, but they are not significant.
> This is consistent with hypocotyl being the weakest cluster.

```{r symbol-mapping}
mapped <- suppressWarnings(bitr(rownames(obj), fromType = "SYMBOL", toType = "ENTREZID",
                                OrgDb = org.At.tair.db))
c(detected_genes = nrow(obj), with_a_GO_usable_symbol = length(unique(mapped$SYMBOL)))
```

> **A limitation:** only `r round(100 * length(unique(mapped$SYMBOL)) / nrow(obj))`% of the detected
> genes can be matched by gene symbol. The others only have a locus code, such as AT2G45180, and are
> silently dropped. This is the reason for the *"...% of input gene IDs are fail to map"* warnings.
> Matching by TAIR locus ID (`keyType = "TAIR"`) instead would keep many more genes. The original
> analysis has the same limitation.

## GSEA: Cotyledon vs Germinating seed

The ranking is the fold change from Step 9, so **positive means higher in Cotyledon**. In the plot:

- **activated** terms sit at the top of the ranking (higher in Cotyledon);
- **suppressed** terms sit at the bottom (higher in Germinating seed).

GSEA estimates its p-values by shuffling, so a fixed seed makes the result repeatable.

```{r gsea}
ranked <- sort(setNames(de$avg_log2FC, de$gene), decreasing = TRUE)
set.seed(123)
gsea <- gseGO(ranked, OrgDb = org.At.tair.db, keyType = "SYMBOL", ont = "BP",
              minGSSize = 10, maxGSSize = 500, pvalueCutoff = 0.05, seed = TRUE, verbose = FALSE)
n_gsea_raw <- nrow(gsea)
gsea <- simplify(gsea, cutoff = 0.7)

as.data.frame(gsea)[, c("Description", "setSize", "NES", "p.adjust")] %>%
  mutate(NES = round(NES, 2), p.adjust = formatC(p.adjust, format = "g", digits = 2)) %>%
  knitr::kable(row.names = FALSE)
```

```{r gsea-plot, fig.width = 8, fig.height = 5}
dotplot(gsea, split = ".sign") + facet_grid(. ~ .sign)
gseaplot2(gsea, geneSetID = 1, title = gsea$Description[1])
```

**Interpretation:** the clearest result is **"photosynthesis, light reaction"** at the top of the
ranking (NES ≈ 3.5): photosynthesis genes are higher in cotyledon, as expected. GSEA finds
`r n_gsea_raw` terms before simplifying and `r nrow(gsea)` after (the original: 22 and 8). All of
them are "activated". Terms such as "biological_process" and "cellular process" sit at the root of
the GO tree and say little on their own.

> **Why are there no "suppressed" terms, even though 49 genes are up in germinating seed?** GSEA
> here only sees the 331 genes that passed the pre-filters in Step 9, and many of them have no GO
> symbol. That gives it little power. Running `FindMarkers` with `logfc.threshold = 0` and
> `min.pct = 0` and ranking all genes would be a better input. That is a natural next step.

# Step 11: Gradients from the shoot apical meristem

**The question:** does gene expression change gradually with distance from the SAM (a gradient), or
switch sharply (a boundary), or not depend on distance at all?

## Separating the seedling pieces

The capture area holds several separate pieces. A distance between bins on different pieces means
nothing, so I first group bins by **position only** (k-means on x and y, 8 groups). Then I keep the
piece that contains the most SAM bins.

```{r pieces}
library(mgcv)
coords <- GetTissueCoordinates(obj)
if ("cell" %in% colnames(coords)) rownames(coords) <- coords$cell

genes_grad <- c("CYP78A5", "AFO", "ANT", "CAB1", "RBCS1A")
df <- FetchData(obj, vars = genes_grad)
df$x <- coords[rownames(df), "x"]
df$y <- coords[rownames(df), "y"]
df$tissue <- Idents(obj)[rownames(df)]

set.seed(123)   # k-means starts from random centres
df$piece <- factor(kmeans(df[, c("x", "y")], centers = 8)$cluster)
table(df$piece, df$tissue)
```

```{r pieces-plot, fig.width = 7, fig.height = 7}
ggplot(df, aes(x, y, colour = piece)) + geom_point(size = 0.8) +
  coord_fixed() + scale_y_reverse() + theme_minimal() +
  ggtitle("Bins grouped into pieces by position (k-means)")
```

```{r shoot-piece}
p <- names(which.max(table(df$piece[df$tissue == "SAM"])))   # the piece containing the SAM
shoot <- droplevels(subset(df, piece == p))

# Coordinates are in image pixels. The scale-factor file says how many µm one pixel is.
# Check: neighbouring 8 µm bins are 29.2 px apart, and 29.2 px × 0.274 µm/px = 8 µm.
um_per_px <- jsonlite::fromJSON(
  "data/binned_outputs/square_008um/spatial/scalefactors_json.json")$microns_per_pixel

centre <- colMeans(shoot[shoot$tissue == "SAM", c("x", "y")])
shoot$dist_um <- sqrt((shoot$x - centre[1])^2 + (shoot$y - centre[2])^2) * um_per_px

shoot %>% group_by(tissue) %>%
  summarise(bins = n(), mean_distance_um = round(mean(dist_um))) %>%
  arrange(mean_distance_um) %>% knitr::kable()
```

**Check:** the SAM piece holds 80 cotyledon, 45 germinating-seed, 51 hypocotyl and 37 SAM bins
(the original: 80, 44, 51, 38). The tissues line up by distance from the SAM in the same order as in
the original: SAM, then germinating seed, cotyledon and hypocotyl. I report distances in µm instead
of pixels so they mean something physically.

```{r shoot-plot, fig.width = 6, fig.height = 7}
ggplot(shoot, aes(x, y, colour = tissue)) + geom_point(size = 2) +
  coord_fixed() + scale_y_reverse() + theme_minimal() +
  ggtitle(paste("Piece", p, ": the shoot"))
```

## Fitting a smooth curve (GAM) for each gene

A GAM (generalised additive model) fits a smooth curve of expression against distance, without
assuming that the relationship is a straight line.

- `k = 4` limits how wiggly the curve can be, so it cannot chase noise.
- The **p-value** tests whether the curve is flat.
- **Deviance explained** is the share of the bin-to-bin variation that distance accounts for.

```{r gam}
gam_results <- do.call(rbind, lapply(genes_grad, function(g) {
  fit <- summary(gam(as.formula(paste(g, "~ s(dist_um, k = 4)")), data = shoot))
  data.frame(gene = g,
             p_value = format.pval(fit$s.table[1, "p-value"], digits = 2),
             deviance_explained = paste0(round(100 * fit$dev.expl, 1), "%"))
}))
knitr::kable(gam_results)
```

```{r gam-plot, fig.width = 13, fig.height = 4.5}
plot_gene <- function(g) {
  ggplot(shoot, aes(dist_um, .data[[g]])) +
    geom_point(aes(colour = tissue), alpha = 0.6) +
    geom_smooth(method = "gam", formula = y ~ s(x, k = 4), colour = "black") +
    labs(title = g, x = "Distance from SAM centre (µm)", y = "log-normalised expression") +
    theme_minimal()
}
(plot_gene("AFO") | plot_gene("ANT") | plot_gene("CAB1")) + plot_layout(guides = "collect")
```

**How to read the curves:** a cliff means a sharp boundary, a slope means a gradient, and a flat
line means distance from the SAM does not matter.

- **AFO** (FILAMENTOUS FLOWER / YABBY1) is expressed only in bins within about 100 µm of the SAM
  centre, mostly in SAM bins, and is absent further away. This is a sharp, local pattern, as
  expected for a gene that marks the young leaf primordia beside the meristem.
- **ANT** (AINTEGUMENTA) shows the same kind of pattern, expressed only within about 60 µm of the
  SAM centre, in SAM and germinating-seed bins. The curve is significant
  (p = `r gam_results$p_value[gam_results$gene == "ANT"]`, the same value as the original) but
  weaker than for AFO, because ANT is detected in fewer bins. The original describes ANT as a
  "modest gradient". In this plot it looks more like a small local domain than a gentle slope.
- **CAB1** has no significant relationship with distance
  (p = `r gam_results$p_value[gam_results$gene == "CAB1"]`; the original: 0.135). It is lower in
  SAM bins than in cotyledon and hypocotyl bins, but it is zero in many bins at every distance, so
  the curve stays flat overall. Photosynthesis genes follow light and chloroplasts rather than the
  developmental axis. RBCS1A, another photosynthesis gene, behaves the same way.

> **Honest note:** distance explains less than 20% of the variation for every gene. Look at the
> row of points along zero at the bottom of each plot: in 8 µm bins most genes are not detected in
> most bins. The GAM treats those zeros as real measurements, which pulls the curves down and
> weakens the fit. The patterns are real, but they are trends, not tight curves. Modelling whether
> a gene is detected at all (a binomial GAM), or using 16 µm bins, would handle this better.

## This run compared with the original

| What | Original | This run |
|---|---|---|
| Genes × bins loaded | 31,109 × 7,356 | `r format(n_genes_raw, big.mark = ",")` × `r format(n_bins_raw, big.mark = ",")` |
| Genes × bins after QC | 17,852 × 1,516 | `r format(nrow(obj), big.mark = ",")` × `r format(ncol(obj), big.mark = ",")` |
| Clusters | 7 | `r length(cluster_sizes)` |
| Top spatially variable gene (Moran's I) | EXT3 (0.791) | `r rownames(svg)[1]` (`r round(svg[1, "MoransI_observed"], 3)`) |
| AGP31 rank among spatially variable genes | 2nd (from 35 genes only) | `r which(rownames(svg) == "AGP31")`th (from all 3,000) |
| Cotyledon vs germinating seed: genes tested | 330 (reported as "DEGs") | `r nrow(de)` |
| ... significant with \|log2FC\| > 1 | not reported | `r sum(de$sig != "Not significant")` |
| GO terms for hypocotyl (ORA) | 5 (from 2 genes) | `r sum(as.data.frame(ora)$Cluster == "hypocotyl")` |
| GSEA terms after simplifying | 8 | `r nrow(gsea)` |
| ANT gradient p-value | 0.00026 | `r gam_results$p_value[gam_results$gene == "ANT"]` |
| CAB1 gradient p-value | 0.135 | `r gam_results$p_value[gam_results$gene == "CAB1"]` |

Everything up to clustering is identical. The later differences come from two sources: bugs in the
original scripts (explained below), and small changes between software versions.

## Bugs fixed in the original scripts

| Problem in the original | Effect | Fix used here |
|---|---|---|
| `06_SVG_detection.R` contains pasted console output (line 41) | The script does not run (syntax error) | Removed |
| `06` uses `top_svg` without ever creating it | Error | Defined from the sorted Moran's I table |
| `06` writes to a hard-coded path on the author's computing cluster | Error on any other computer | Relative path `results/` |
| `05` re-runs `ScaleData()` on only the ~35 heat-map genes | Moran's I can then only test those 35 genes | Scale variable genes + heat-map genes |
| The markers file stores cluster numbers, but `08` filters by tissue names | Tissue-specific ORA cut-offs silently do nothing | Add a `tissue` column and filter on it |
| `09` assumes k-means "piece 1" is the shoot | Breaks when k-means numbers the pieces differently | Pick the piece with the most SAM bins |
| Volcano plots use `-log10(0)` | Points with p = 0 vanish | Add `1e-300` before taking the log |
| `FindMarkers` row counts reported as "DEGs" | Overstates the number of differentially expressed genes | Report tested, significant, and significant + two-fold separately |

## Problems hit along the way, and how they were solved

| Symptom | Cause | Fix |
|---|---|---|
| `cannot open file` / `No such file or directory` | Commands were run from the wrong folder | Open the `.Rproj` file so the working directory is the project folder |
| Package installation stopped with a timeout | R's 60-second download limit | `options(timeout = 3600)`, and install before downloading the data |
| `Cannot find the following identities in the object: Root` | The clusters had not been renamed yet | Run the renaming chunk; check with `levels(Idents(obj))` |
| `object 'tissue' not found` in Step 10 | `markers` was made before renaming | Add `markers$tissue` right after `RenameIdents()` |
| `unable to find an inherited method for function 'select'` | clusterProfiler's dependencies mask dplyr's `select()` | Write `dplyr::select()` |
| Knitting reinstalled packages and re-downloaded 768 MB | The setup chunks ran on every knit | `eval = FALSE` on those chunks; run them once by hand |

## Limitations

- **One section of one sample.** Bins are not biological replicates, so the statistics describe
  this slide, not seedlings in general.
- **Bins are not cells.** A bin on a tissue border can mix cell types.
- **The tissue names rest on a handful of marker genes.** "hypocotyl" is the weakest label: it has
  few specific markers and no enriched GO terms.
- **GO analysis loses genes.** Only about 42% of detected genes can be matched by gene symbol.

## Ideas for next steps

All four are tried in the follow-up notebook, [follow_up_analyses.md](follow_up_analyses.md).

- Repeat the analysis with 16 µm bins (`bin.size = 16`). Are the same tissues found, with less noise?
- Try `SCTransform()` for normalisation, or BANKSY for clustering that also uses position.
- Run GSEA on **all** genes, and match genes by TAIR locus ID to keep more of them.
- Fit the gradient along the **root** (meristematic tissue → elongation zone → root) instead of the
  shoot.
